domain_assessment.domain: Nuclear-power refueling outage maintenance planning and operational coordination
domain_assessment.objective: Sequence maintenance work, allocate constrained craft-hours, protect the outage critical path, and support justified return to service before mode-change hold points
domain_assessment.incident_type: Outage-planning and maintenance-anomaly decision sequence involving a feedwater isolation valve, crew allocation, adjacent pump vibration, and return-to-service concurrence

decision_points.summary: The participant elevated FW-IV-204 to top-tier rework priority during outage scoping.
evidence_before: Two prior condition reports had been closed as acceptable-as-found.
There was no adverse local trend in leak rate.
Other work orders had comparable or higher condition-report severity ratings.
A vivid account of a sister-unit valve failure involving nearly the same valve type was recently recalled.
evidence_after: FW-IV-204 was moved to top-tier priority.
The participant did not retrieve updated local trend data specifically to test the sister-unit-driven concern.
The valve work itself was completed without the feared failure.
goals_constraints: Prevent a potentially schedule-threatening valve failure.
Prioritize approximately 140 concurrent work orders in a 21-day outage window.
alternatives: Rank the valve according to documented local condition-report trend and severity.
Pull current leak-rate data before finalizing the rank.
Assign an intermediate priority while monitoring the valve.
decision_points.decision_basis: The recalled sister-unit failure was weighted more heavily than flat local history and comparative work-order severity.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate pre-outage planning pressure, but the participant reports more breathing room than at the crew-assignment decision.
decision_points.uncertainty: The local condition was not clearly urgent, while the probability that the sister-unit event generalized to this valve was not established.

decision_points.summary: The participant selected the first crew configuration that met minimum schedule and safety requirements.
evidence_before: Several technically feasible crew configurations existed.
Options differed in overtime, fatigue limits, and downstream sequencing.
The daily craft-hour budget was substantially consumed.
The Outage Manager required a decision within one hour.
evidence_after: The selected configuration produced a minor later sequencing conflict with an unrelated pump job.
A later review identified a marginally better configuration that would have avoided that friction.
The conflict did not materially disrupt the overall outage schedule.
goals_constraints: Respond to a one-hour management deadline.
alternatives: Compare all three or four configurations on overtime, fatigue, and downstream sequencing.
Escalate the time-versus-optimization trade-off to the Outage Manager.
decision_points.decision_basis: The first option clearing minimum schedule and safety thresholds was selected rather than continuing the search for a better configuration.
decision_points.time_pressure: High and explicit: decision required within one hour.
decision_points.uncertainty: The downstream effects of each feasible configuration were not fully compared before selection.

decision_points.summary: The participant attributed an adjacent pump-bearing vibration anomaly to residual misalignment from valve rework and closed the anomaly after reviewing selectively requested vibration data.
evidence_before: Valve rework had recently occurred in the adjacent area.
A mild pump-bearing vibration anomaly was observed during post-maintenance functional testing.
A lubrication-log entry for the bearing was available in the system.
The bearing's full trend history was also available.
evidence_after: The participant requested immediate vibration readings associated with a misalignment signature.
Readings consistent with the misalignment theory were treated as sufficient to document the anomaly as resolved.
The lubrication log and full trend history were not requested at that time.
The system engineer reviewed the trend history later.
goals_constraints: Determine whether the vibration anomaly required further investigation.
Support safe and timely completion of post-maintenance testing.
Avoid unnecessarily broad diagnostic work during an outage.
alternatives: Review the lubrication log before closing the anomaly.
Review the full bearing trend history.
Seek evidence that would distinguish misalignment from lubrication-related or pre-existing bearing conditions.
Keep the anomaly open pending wider engineering review.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant searched for and accepted evidence consistent with the initial misalignment hypothesis while not seeking available records that could challenge it.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate; the participant reports the decision had more breathing room than the crew-assignment episode.
decision_points.uncertainty: The vibration signature alone did not uniquely establish residual misalignment as the cause.

decision_points.summary: The participant concurred with return to service after formal closure of condition reports, written engineering concurrence, and a direct walkdown with operations.
evidence_before: Valve and adjacent-pump condition reports were formally closed.
The system engineer had provided written concurrence.
The participant completed a walkdown with operations.
The earlier vibration anomaly had been considered in the documented closeout.
evidence_after: The participant concurred with return to service.
No additional monitoring period was requested before mode change.
goals_constraints: Return the unit to service without unjustified delay.
Avoid holding the unit without a specific technical basis.
alternatives: Request an additional monitoring period before mode change.
Hold return to service pending further review.
Concur based on the completed technical and operational controls.
decision_points.decision_basis: Formal engineering concurrence, closed records, and direct field observation all aligned; the participant did not identify a specific technical reason to delay.
decision_points.time_pressure: General outage schedule pressure was present, but no acute decision deadline is described.
decision_points.uncertainty: Residual uncertainty from the earlier anomaly remained, but the available formal and field evidence was described as convergent.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “The sister-unit story, honestly... it involved almost the exact same valve type. That stuck with me... So I moved it up.” Also: “I didn't pull updated numbers specifically to test whether the concern was warranted.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Priority-ranking reconstruction, following the interviewer’s question about what tipped FW-IV-204 to top-tier priority.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: A recent, vivid, and consequential sister-unit failure was treated as especially diagnostic of local risk despite flat local leak-rate history, prior acceptable-as-found reports, and competing work orders with equal or higher documented severity. The participant then did not retrieve updated local trend evidence to test the salience-driven concern.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A similar failure at a sister unit can legitimately justify precautionary escalation in a high-consequence nuclear setting. However, the text supplies the necessary differentiator: the local evidence was explicitly unremarkable and the participant states that the vivid account, rather than a fresh local evaluation, tipped the ranking.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required for support. A quantitative comparison of local failure indicators with the sister-unit event would further distinguish prudent risk transfer from availability weighting, but is not necessary here.

revision.location: Decision point 1, participant answers beginning “The sister-unit story, honestly” and “No, not really.”
revision.current_defect: None material. The episode contains a distinct priority decision, a vivid recalled incident, contrary local trend information, and an explicit failure to re-check that local information.
preserve: The sister-unit incident as the vivid recalled source
Flat local condition-report and leak-rate history
The participant’s failure to pull updated local trend data
avoid_creating: A second availability episode at the crew-configuration, vibration, or return-to-service decision points
An explicit textbook statement naming availability bias

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I looked at the first configuration that met minimum schedule and safety requirements, confirmed it cleared those bars, and locked it in.” Also: “comparing all the variables... for three or four configurations would have eaten time I didn't have.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Crew-configuration discussion under the one-hour Outage Manager deadline.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: Under explicit time and cognitive-capacity constraints, the participant applied a satisfactory threshold—minimum schedule and safety requirements—and selected the first option meeting it rather than conducting a full comparison of feasible alternatives. This is a discrete satisficing decision in resource allocation.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Rapid selection of a safe, schedule-compliant option can be justified operationally under a one-hour deadline. The requested bounded-rationality mechanism is nevertheless supported because the participant explicitly identifies multiple feasible options, a foregone full comparison, and first-satisfactory-option selection.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. The later identification of a marginally better option corroborates, but does not itself establish, the satisficing mechanism.

revision.location: Decision point 2, participant answers beginning “We were maybe two-thirds through” and “I thought about it.”
revision.current_defect: None material. The account clearly separates the decision threshold, feasible option set, time constraint, and truncated search.
preserve: Selection of the first satisfactory configuration
avoid_creating: Framing the marginally better later option as proof that the original decision was irrational
Adding a second satisficing episode to priority ranking or anomaly diagnosis

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I asked for the immediate vibration readings... whether the signature matched a misalignment pattern. They looked consistent with that, so I documented the anomaly as resolved.” Also: “I didn't pull [the lubrication log] because the misalignment explanation already fit what I was seeing, and I didn't feel a need to widen the search once I had a reading that matched.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Vibration-anomaly reconstruction, especially the answers on requested vibration readings, lubrication logs, and trend history.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: After forming a residual-misalignment theory, the participant sought immediate vibration readings specifically capable of matching that theory, accepted matching readings as sufficient, and did not request available lubrication and historical-trend records because the existing theory already appeared to fit. The evidence-selection restriction is explicitly tied to the pre-formed explanation.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Immediate vibration readings may be an appropriate first diagnostic source, and the participant later obtained engineering concurrence before return to service. The episode remains confirmation bias because closure occurred without reviewing available potentially disconfirming sources expressly because the favored explanation already fit.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. Identification of what the lubrication entry actually showed would strengthen causal diagnosis, but confirmation bias is supported by the selective search and stopping rule rather than by proof that lubrication was the true cause.

revision.location: Decision point 3, participant answers beginning “I asked for the immediate vibration readings” and “In hindsight, yes.”
revision.current_defect: None material. The account identifies the initial theory, confirmatory evidence request, omitted available records, and reasoning for not widening the investigation.
preserve: The targeted request for a matching vibration signature
The unrequested lubrication log and full trend history
The neutral evidence basis for decision point 4
avoid_creating: Reintroducing selective evidence review during the return-to-service decision
Stating that omitted records definitively disproved misalignment
Adding a second confirmation-bias episode through the later walkdown or engineering concurrence

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “My first thought was residual misalignment from the rework we'd just done.” Also: “I didn't feel a need to widen the search once I had a reading that matched.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The initial misalignment explanation may have anchored subsequent diagnostic processing and contributed to early closure of the investigation.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Residual misalignment was a temporally and physically plausible initial hypothesis after nearby maintenance. The stronger and more specific supported mechanism is confirmation bias, because the text foregrounds selective evidence request and omission of disconfirming sources rather than mere fixation on a first impression.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “When we reviewed it afterward, there was a configuration that would have avoided that friction. Marginally better, not dramatically.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The later outcome could invite retrospective evaluation of the original crew-allocation decision based on the sequencing conflict.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant does not use the later result to claim the initial decision was unreasonable; instead, the account describes the original time constraint and the limited material consequence.

nonbias_cues.cue: Six years as outage coordinator plus four years as a planner
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Experience is contextual expertise. It does not by itself show overconfidence, rigidity, or any distorted reasoning process.
Time pressure is an organizational constraint. It supports the context for decision point 2 but is not itself a cognitive bias.

nonbias_cues.cue: Minor later sequencing conflict after crew assignment
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: An unfavorable or suboptimal outcome does not establish a bias. The bounded-rationality classification rests on the documented first-satisfactory-option search process, not on the later conflict.

nonbias_cues.cue: Initial attribution of vibration to nearby valve rework
nonbias_cues.location: Opening account of the vibration anomaly and decision point 3
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Temporal proximity can supply a reasonable working hypothesis. It becomes bias-relevant only because the participant subsequently limited evidence seeking after finding confirmatory readings.

nonbias_cues.cue: Return-to-service concurrence after written engineering approval and direct walkdown
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant cites convergent formal, technical, and direct-observation evidence and explains why additional delay lacked a specific technical basis. This is a justified operational judgment, not blind deference or normalization of deviance.

nonbias_cues.cue: Retrospective statement that the lubrication log might have changed the review
nonbias_cues.location: Interviewer’s hypothetical probe after decision point 4
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The statement is hindsight reflection, not a separate decision or additional confirmation-bias occurrence.

causal_claims.claim: The sister-unit failure story caused FW-IV-204 to be elevated in priority.
causal_claims.support: The participant explicitly states that the story “tipped it” and led to moving the valve up.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately supported as a self-reported causal account of the participant’s reasoning; it does not establish that the higher ranking was objectively unjustified.

causal_claims.claim: Residual misalignment from valve rework caused the pump-bearing vibration anomaly.
causal_claims.support: The participant cites sequence and vibration readings consistent with a misalignment pattern.
causal_claims.assessment: Weakly supported as a causal diagnosis. The evidence is compatible with, but does not uniquely identify, misalignment; lubrication and long-term trend records were not reviewed before closeout.

causal_claims.claim: The selected crew configuration created the later pump-job sequencing conflict.
causal_claims.support: The participant reports that the configuration created minor friction and a later review found an alternative that would have avoided it.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately supported operational counterfactual, though the account does not provide a full dependency analysis of other schedule factors.

causal_claims.claim: Holding the unit longer would not have been justified.
causal_claims.support: Closed condition reports, written engineering concurrence, and a clean walkdown aligned.
causal_claims.assessment: Reasonably supported as a decision justification, not as proof that additional monitoring would have had no operational value.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The temporal fact that maintenance occurred near the pump and the observation that vibration readings matched a misalignment signature may be mistaken for conclusive causal proof. Alternative causes were not checked before closure.

The later sequencing conflict is consistent with the selected configuration contributing to friction, but does not on its own prove that the original decision process was deficient or that all other operational factors were irrelevant.

causal_audit.changed_variable: The interview contains informal retrospective counterfactuals rather than a designed paired-scenario counterfactual: ranking FW-IV-204 purely by documented trend, selecting a different crew configuration, or having the lubrication log immediately available.
held_constant: The participant’s role and outage setting
The basic valve-work and vibration-anomaly chronology
The return-to-service documentation and walkdown described in the actual account
causal_audit.explanation: The narrative appropriately distinguishes the participant’s subjective reasoning from several later outcomes, but the misalignment explanation remains underdetermined because relevant alternative evidence was omitted at the time. The informal hypotheticals are not treated as proof of causation and do not create a formal counterfactual-condition failure.

global_revision_constraints: Preserve the separation between priority ranking, crew allocation, anomaly investigation, and return-to-service judgment.
Do not convert the participant’s naturalistic explanations into explicit bias labels.
Do not treat the later mild scheduling conflict or the ultimate successful valve work as proof of cognitive bias.
Keep decision point 4 evidence-based and free of additional selective-evidence or salience-driven reasoning.
